content:
The Problem

In precision analog optical receivers, noise on the DC power rails couples directly into high-gain operational amplifier stages and corrupts microvolt-level sensor signals. For this EC EN 340 milestone, our circuit was powered by a single $3.3\text{V}$ DC voltage source (V1) contaminated with a $30\text{mV}$ AC ripple at $1481\text{Hz}$—sitting right inside our target $1250\text{Hz}\text{–}3666\text{Hz}$ signal passband. Furthermore, the dual-rail operational amplifiers required clean, symmetric $+1.65\text{V}$ (vp) and $-1.65\text{V}$ (vn) supply rails while strictly preserving the starter netlist’s V1, I1, and R1 components.

My Contribution

I designed and implemented a two-part power conditioning and rail-splitting architecture in NGspice:

  1. 3-Stage Cascaded RC Low-Pass Ripple Filter: Ahead of the voltage divider, I placed three low-impedance series resistors ($R_{24} = 10\ \Omega$, $R_{11} = 10\ \Omega$, $R_4 = 10\ \Omega$) paired with large shunt decoupling capacitors ($C_{22} = 159\ \mu\text{F}$ and $C_9 = 159\ \mu\text{F}$). With an individual stage corner frequency of $f_c = \frac{1}{2\pi (10\ \Omega)(159\ \mu\text{F})} \approx 100\text{Hz}$, this cascade heavily attenuates the $1481\text{Hz}$ power-supply ripple before it reaches the rail splitter.
  2. Symmetric Virtual-Ground Rail Splitter & Multi-Decade Bypassing: I constructed a balanced $100\text{k}\Omega$ voltage divider ($R_2 = 100\text{k}\Omega$, $R_3 = 100\text{k}\Omega$) and strategically placed the system reference ground (0V) directly between $R_2$ and $R_3$. I stabilized both the positive (vp) and negative (vn) rails using parallel bulk ($C_1, C_2 = 1\text{mF}$) and high-frequency ($C_3, C_4 = 1\ \mu\text{F}$) bypass capacitors to ground.

The Result

  • Generated rock-solid, symmetric $v_p = +1.65\text{V}$ and $v_n = -1.65\text{V}$ supply rails from the single $3.3\text{V}$ source with minimal static current draw.
  • Eliminated the $30\text{mV}$, $1481\text{Hz}$ power-line ripple from the op-amp power pins, preventing in-band power supply modulation from masking the $1\text{pA}$ photodiode signal.

What This Artifact Demonstrates

  • Power Integrity & Decoupling Design: Combining low-pass RC filtering with multi-decade capacitor bypassing ($1\text{mF}$ and $1\ \mu\text{F}$) to suppress in-band supply noise.
  • Reference Node & Virtual Ground Synthesis: Establishing dual bipolar supply rails ($\pm 1.65\text{V}$) from a unipolar source by strategically defining the circuit ground node.
  • Constraint-Driven SPICE Modeling: Extending a constrained starter netlist (V1, I1, R1) without introducing floating nodes or DC path errors.

Evidence of Revision (Based on Feedback)

  • Initial Draft vs. Revised Design: In my initial schematic layout, the $3.3\text{V}$ supply divider lacked multi-stage series RC decoupling ahead of R2/R3, allowing the $1481\text{Hz}$ ripple on V1 to modulate vp and vn. Based on simulation diagnostics and lab feedback, I added the 3-stage $10\ \Omega / 159\ \mu\text{F}$ low-pass filter cascade and paired the $1\text{mF}$ bulk capacitors with $1\ \mu\text{F}$ bypass capacitors.
  • Portfolio Documentation Revision: Earlier versions of my portfolio merged this rail-splitter work into a short paragraph inside Artifact 2 without explaining why the $1481\text{Hz}$ ripple was so dangerous (it lies directly inside the $1250\text{Hz}\text{–}3666\text{Hz}$ passband). I revised this into a standalone artifact with explicit Problem, Contribution, Result, and Demonstrated Competency sections.

Design Journey Note

  • Start of Semester vs. Now: At the beginning of the semester, I treated voltage sources in circuit diagrams as ideal, noiseless batteries. Through this project, I learned how real-world power supplies inject in-band ripple into sensitive analog front-ends—and I can now design multi-stage RC decoupling networks and split-rail virtual grounds from scratch.

Circuit Schematic

content:
The Problem

This EC EN 340 design challenge required isolating an ultra-weak $1\text{pA}$ ($2000\text{Hz}$) optical signal (Is) from severe multi-source interference using at most two operational amplifiers. Specifically, the photodiode sensing node (in) was simultaneously driven by:

  • A $1\text{mA}$ DC ambient light offset (In1),
  • A $400\text{nA}$ low-frequency interference source at $100\text{Hz}$ (In2),
  • A $400\text{nA}$ high-frequency interference source at $20\text{kHz}$ (In3), and
  • A $1481\text{Hz}$ power-supply ripple source (V1).

Because the interfering currents were $400{,}000\times$ to $10^9\times$ larger than the $1\text{pA}$ target current, the circuit had to provide massive in-band amplification across the target $1250\text{Hz}$ to $3666\text{Hz}$ frequency window while aggressively rejecting all out-of-band frequencies.

My Contribution

I architected a multi-stage hybrid passive-and-active bandpass filter chain centered on the $1000\text{Hz}$ to $10\text{kHz}$ corner window:

  1. 3-Stage Input Passive RC High-Pass Filter: Configured three cascaded high-pass poles ($C_{27}, C_{26}, C_{25} = 15\text{nF}$ and $R_{29}, R_{28}, R_{27} = 10.6\text{k}\Omega$) with a corner frequency of $f_L = \frac{1}{2\pi (10.6\text{k}\Omega)(15\text{nF})} \approx 1001\text{Hz}$ to completely block the $1\text{mA}$ DC current and sharply attenuate the $100\text{Hz}$ photodiode hum before amplification.
  2. Two Cascaded High-Gain Inverting Active Bandpass Op-Amp Stages (X1, X2): Designed each op-amp stage with an input series network ($R_{25}, R_{26} = 1\text{k}\Omega$ and $C_{23}, C_{24} = 159\text{nF}$, $f_L \approx 1001\text{Hz}$) and a parallel RC feedback loop ($R_{30}, R_{31} = 1\text{M}\Omega$ and $C_{31}, C_{32} = 15.9\text{pF}$, $f_H \approx 10.01\text{kHz}$). Each stage delivers an mid-band gain magnitude of $|A_v| = \frac{1\text{M}\Omega}{1\text{k}\Omega} = 1000\text{ V/V}$ ($60\text{dB}$), yielding $120\text{dB}$ ($10^6\text{ V/V}$) total passband gain.
  3. 3-Stage Output Passive RC Low-Pass Filter: Added three cascaded low-pass poles ($R_{32}, R_{33}, R_{34} = 1.6\text{k}\Omega$ and $C_{28}, C_{29}, C_{30} = 10\text{nF}$) at $f_H = \frac{1}{2\pi (1.6\text{k}\Omega)(10\text{nF})} \approx 9947\text{Hz}$ to strip out the $20\text{kHz}$ photodiode noise at the output (out).

The Result

  • Successfully amplified the $1\text{pA}$ ($2000\text{Hz}$) signal across the required $1250\text{Hz}\text{–}3666\text{Hz}$ passband into a clean, measurable output voltage waveform.
  • Achieved steep 4th-order high-pass and 4th-order low-pass roll-off per active/passive cascade, suppressing the $0\text{Hz}$ DC offset, $100\text{Hz}$ hum, and $20\text{kHz}$ interference without saturating either op-amp against the $\pm 1.65\text{V}$ rails.

What This Artifact Demonstrates

  • Multi-Pole Filter Synthesis & Bode Analysis: Selecting exact standard resistor and capacitor values to place lower ($1\text{kHz}$) and upper ($10\text{kHz}$) poles symmetrically around a target passband.
  • High-Gain Cascaded Amplifier Staging: Distributing $120\text{dB}$ of gain across two inverting bandpass op-amps while stripping DC and out-of-band energy prior to the first gain stage to avoid rail saturation.
  • SPICE AC Sweep & Signal-to-Noise Verification: Translating physical photodiode interference constraints into an end-to-end verified NGspice topology.

Evidence of Revision (Based on Feedback)

  • Technical Filter Revision: My earliest design relied primarily on the op-amps’ single-pole feedback networks, which did not provide a steep enough roll-off to suppress the $400\text{nA}$ noise sources at $100\text{Hz}$ and $20\text{kHz}$ ($54\text{dB}$ stronger than the $1\text{pA}$ signal). Based on simulation feedback, I added the 3-stage passive RC high-pass cascade at the input and the 3-stage passive RC low-pass cascade at the output, dramatically sharpening the passband skirts.
  • Portfolio Communication Revision: Based on portfolio feedback, I expanded my original two-sentence summary into a full engineering breakdown detailing the exact component values ($15\text{nF}/10.6\text{k}\Omega$, $1\text{M}\Omega/15.9\text{pF}$, $1.6\text{k}\Omega/10\text{nF}$), gain calculations ($60\text{dB}$ per stage), and quantitative results.

Design Journey Note

  • What I Can Now Do That I Could Not Do at the Beginning of the Semester: At the start of the semester, I could not design a multi-stage filter to recover a picowatt signal buried in noise, nor did I understand why high-pass filtering must precede high-gain amplification. I can now calculate corner frequencies across multiple cascaded stages, prevent DC offset saturation, and transition seamlessly from NGspice simulation to physical breadboard implementation.

content:
The Problem

The objective of this EC EN 340 circuit was to condition the optical sensor signal for an autonomous light-following robot. In a mobile robotics platform, only a single $9\text{V}$ battery (V1 = 9V) and $0\text{V}$ ground are available—there is no negative voltage supply rail. Furthermore, static ambient room lighting creates a large DC photodiode offset, while the robot needs to track a modulated $1\text{kHz}$ target light beacon (I1 = 0.1 mA). Without proper DC blocking and mid-rail biasing, the negative half-cycle of the AC signal immediately clips against the $0\text{V}$ ground rail.

My Contribution

I designed a single-supply, AC-coupled inverting amplifier and signal-conditioning stage in NGspice:

  1. Sensor Transducer & Input AC Coupling: Converted the $0.1\text{mA}$, $1\text{kHz}$ photodiode current (I1) into a voltage across sense resistor $R_1 = 1\text{k}\Omega$, and placed a series coupling capacitor $C_1 = 1\ \mu\text{F}$ ahead of input resistor $R_4 = 10\text{M}\Omega$ to block ambient DC room light.
  2. Mid-Rail Virtual Ground Biasing ($+4.5\text{V}$): Configured op-amp X1 with its supply rails at $9\text{V}$ (vp) and $0\text{V}$ (GND), and constructed a matched $100\text{k}\Omega$ voltage divider ($R_7 = 100\text{k}\Omega$, $R_8 = 100\text{k}\Omega$) to bias the non-inverting input (+) at exactly $+4.5\text{V}$ ($\frac{1}{2}V_{CC}$).
  3. High-Impedance Gain & Output DC Restoration: Set the feedback resistor to $R_5 = 50\text{M}\Omega$ over $R_4 = 10\text{M}\Omega$ for an inverting voltage gain of $|A_v| = \frac{50\text{M}\Omega}{10\text{M}\Omega} = 5\text{ V/V}$, and added an output high-pass AC-coupling stage ($C_2 = 1\ \mu\text{F}$, $R_9 = 1\text{M}\Omega$) to remove the $+4.5\text{V}$ DC bias so the final out signal swings cleanly around $0\text{V}$.

The Result

  • Eliminated single-supply rail clipping by centering the internal op-amp signal swing at $+4.5\text{V}$, allowing maximum peak-to-peak headroom between $0\text{V}$ and $9\text{V}$.
  • Rejected steady-state ambient room lighting via dual AC-coupling capacitors ($C_1, C_2$) while delivering an amplified, unclipped $1\text{kHz}$ output signal (out) ready for downstream robot detection circuitry.

What This Artifact Demonstrates

  • Single-Supply Analog Engineering: Designing op-amp circuits that operate reliably from a single $9\text{V}$ battery using a $\frac{1}{2}V_{CC}$ virtual ground reference.
  • Input & Output AC Coupling: Using series blocking capacitors ($C_1, C_2$) to isolate DC operating points between sensor, amplifier, and load stages.
  • Practical Embedded Sensor Interfacing: Translating real-world robotics hardware constraints (battery power + ambient room light interference) into a working analog front-end.

Evidence of Revision (Based on Feedback)

  • Circuit Design Revision: During initial testing, attempting to amplify the photodiode signal without the output RC restoration network ($C_2 = 1\ \mu\text{F}$, $R_9 = 1\text{M}\Omega$) left the output riding on a $+4.5\text{V}$ DC offset. Based on lab feedback, I added the output coupling stage so downstream stages receive a true $0\text{V}$-centered AC waveform, and verified that $R_7/R_8$ ($100\text{k}\Omega$) held the virtual ground stable under load.
  • Portfolio Narrative Revision: I revised this artifact write-up to explicitly separate The Problem, My Contribution, The Result, and What This Artifact Demonstrates, and added quantitative analysis of thegain ($R_5/R_4 = 50\text{M}\Omega/10\text{M}\Omega = 5\text{ V/V}$) and biasing network.

Design Journey Note

  • What I Can Now Do That I Could Not Do at the Beginning of the Semester: At the start of the semester, I did not know how an op-amp could amplify an AC signal swinging positive and negative when powered only by a $9\text{V}$ battery and $0\text{V}$ ground. I can now establish a stable mid-rail virtual ground ($+4.5\text{V}$), select biasing resistors that prevent loading, and use AC coupling to interface single-supply analog filters with embedded robotics hardware.

Circuit Schematic
description: Designing a 9V single-supply AC-coupled transimpedance/inverting amplifier with a +4.5V virtual ground bias for an autonomous light-following robot.
title: Artifact 3: Single-Supply Light-Following Robot Filter & Virtual Ground Biasing

content:
The Problem

When translating complex multi-stage schematics into text-based NGspice netlists in EC EN 340, small node-numbering or grounding errors can silently kill an entire signal chain without throwing a syntax error. Specifically, in our optical receiver simulation, we were required to strictly preserve the starter netlist’s V1, I1, and R1 components and interconnections while integrating a rail splitter, two active bandpass op-amps, and six passive RC filter stages. A common failure mode in early drafts was inadvertently grounding series coupling capacitors (C6/C7 and C23/C24) or mis-referencing the op-amp power and virtual ground nodes, which shunted the target AC signal to ground or locked the op-amp rails.

My Contribution

I led a systematic netlist verification and topology debugging audit across the schematic and SPICE code:

  1. Node-by-Node Netlist & Capacitor Routing Audit: I traced every netlist node between the schematic and SPICE code, verifying that series coupling and high-pass capacitors (C6/C7, C23–C27) were routed strictly inline between stages rather than tied to node 0 (ground), and confirming that shunt low-pass capacitors (C28–C30) and rail bypass capacitors (C1–C4) terminated properly at node 0.
  2. Starter-Code Constraint Compliance (V1, I1, R1): I verified that the original V1 power source, photodiode current sources (In1–In3, Is), diode D1, and $2500\ \Omega$ sense resistor R1 maintained their exact required node assignments while interfacing cleanly at node in.
  3. Iterative Bode & Transient Verification: I used NGspice simulation outputs to iteratively tune component values across the 3-stage input HPF ($15\text{nF} / 10.6\text{k}\Omega$) and 3-stage output LPF ($1.6\text{k}\Omega / 10\text{nF}$), confirming both DC operating point stability ($\pm 1.65\text{V}$ rails) and AC passband fidelity ($1250\text{Hz}\text{–}3666\text{Hz}$).

The Result

  • Eliminated signal-shunting schematic/netlist bugs by ensuring all coupling capacitors (C6/C7, C23/C24) passed AC signals in series while shunt bypass capacitors routed high-frequency noise to ground.
  • Delivered a verified, reproducible NGspice netlist and schematic that met 100% of the EC EN 340 Milestone 1 specifications and passed automated/lab verification checks.

What This Artifact Demonstrates

  • Systematic Debugging & Root-Cause Analysis: Diagnosing subtle circuit topology bugs (such as series vs. shunt capacitor grounding and virtual-ground reference errors) by correlating SPICE node voltages with circuit theory.
  • Verification Rigor & Constraint Adherence: Modifying complex systems within strict interface rules (preserving legacy/starter components V1, I1, R1)—a critical skill in both hardware engineering and enterprise security infrastructure.
  • Feedback-Driven Engineering Iteration: Using simulation diagnostics and instructor/TA feedback to systematically refine a design from an initial draft to a verified production netlist.

Evidence of Revision (Based on Feedback)

  • Recovering & Expanding Earlier Portfolio Work: In an earlier version of my repository (commit 7b2ba54), my SPICE netlist analysis (“EC EN 340 Artifact 2: SPICE Circuit Simulation”) was overwritten when I added the Light-Following Robot Filter post. Based on portfolio review feedback requiring at least four distinct EC EN 340 artifacts and clear evidence of revision, I restored my netlist debugging and capacitor-routing work (C6/C7 and R2/R3 ground placement) and expanded it into this comprehensive verification artifact.

Design Journey Note

  • What I Can Now Do That I Could Not Do at the Beginning of the Semester: At the start of the semester, a flat SPICE netlist looked like an inscrutable list of node numbers, and when a simulation produced a flat $0\text{V}$ line, I had to guess what was wrong. Today, I can audit netlists systematically—checking DC bias points first, verifying series vs. shunt reactive components, and validating AC frequency responses stage-by-stage.

content:
1. Professional Introduction & Target Role

Target Role: Security Infrastructure Engineer / Data Center Hardware & Systems Engineer

I am Landon Wilmott, a Computer Engineering student at Brigham Young University (BYU) with a minor in Cybersecurity. Alongside my engineering coursework, I supervise student employees in IT support and computer lab maintenance, and I hold CompTIA A+, Network+, and Security+ certifications.

I am actively pursuing Security Infrastructure Engineer and Data Center Hardware / Systems Engineering roles where I can combine my hands-on background in hardware maintenance, analog/digital circuit diagnostics, network virtualization, and systems administration to build resilient, high-availability infrastructure.

2. Organized Table of Contents

  1. Professional Introduction & Target Role
  2. Organized Table of Contents
  3. Selected EC EN 340 Artifacts (4 Artifacts)
    • Artifact 1: Power Supply Rail Splitter & 3-Stage Ripple Decoupling Network
    • Artifact 2: Dual Op-Amp Cascaded Bandpass Noise Filter (1.25 kHz – 3.67 kHz)
    • Artifact 3: Single-Supply Light-Following Robot Filter & Virtual Ground Biasing
    • Artifact 4: NGspice Netlist Verification, Capacitor Grounding Audit & Multi-Pole Revision
  4. Evidence of Revision Based on Feedback
  5. Design Journey Note: Start of Semester vs. Now
  6. Connection to BYU Aims (aims.byu.edu)

3. Selected EC EN 340 Artifacts

Below are four selected engineering artifacts from EC EN 340 (Electronic Circuit Design 1), each structured to highlight The Problem, My Contribution, The Result, and What This Artifact Demonstrates.

Artifact 1: Power Supply Rail Splitter & 3-Stage Ripple Decoupling Network

  • Standalone Write-Up: Open Artifact 1 Full Page →
  • The Problem: Our optical receiver circuit was powered by a single $3.3\text{V}$ DC supply (V1) contaminated with a $30\text{mV}$ AC ripple at $1481\text{Hz}$—directly inside our $1250\text{Hz}\text{–}3666\text{Hz}$ passband—while the operational amplifiers required clean, symmetric $+1.65\text{V}$ (vp) and $-1.65\text{V}$ (vn) dual rails.
  • My Contribution: I designed a 3-stage cascaded RC low-pass decoupling filter ($R_{24}, R_{11}, R_4 = 10\ \Omega$ and $C_{22}, C_9 = 159\ \mu\text{F}$, with stage corner frequency $f_c \approx 100\text{Hz}$) feeding a matched $100\text{k}\Omega$ voltage divider ($R_2, R_3$). To establish symmetric bipolar rails, I placed the system reference ground (0V) directly between $R_2$ and $R_3$ and added parallel multi-decade bypass capacitors ($1\text{mF}$ bulk + $1\ \mu\text{F}$ high-frequency) on both rails.
  • The Result: Produced stable $v_p = +1.65\text{V}$ and $v_n = -1.65\text{V}$ supply rails while heavily attenuating the $1481\text{Hz}$ power-line ripple before it could modulate the high-gain amplifier stages.
  • What This Artifact Demonstrates: Power integrity engineering, virtual ground synthesis, multi-decade capacitor bypassing, and constraint-driven SPICE modeling.

Artifact 2: Dual Op-Amp Cascaded Bandpass Noise Filter (1.25 kHz – 3.67 kHz)

  • Standalone Write-Up: Open Artifact 2 Full Page →
  • The Problem: Using a maximum of two operational amplifiers, isolate an ultra-weak $1\text{pA}$ ($2000\text{Hz}$) photodiode signal (Is) from a $1\text{mA}$ DC offset (In1), two $400\text{nA}$ photodiode noise sources at $100\text{Hz}$ (In2) and $20\text{kHz}$ (In3), and a $1481\text{Hz}$ power supply ripple so that only the $1250\text{Hz}\text{–}3666\text{Hz}$ target band passes through.
  • My Contribution: I designed a hybrid passive-active bandpass chain with lower corner frequency $f_L = 1000\text{Hz}$ and upper corner frequency $f_H = 10\text{kHz}$. This combined a 3-stage passive RC high-pass input filter ($C = 15\text{nF}, R = 10.6\text{k}\Omega$), two cascaded inverting active bandpass op-amps ($R_{in} = 1\text{k}\Omega, C_{in} = 159\text{nF}, R_f = 1\text{M}\Omega, C_f = 15.9\text{pF}$ providing $60\text{dB}$ gain per stage / $120\text{dB}$ total), and a 3-stage passive RC low-pass output filter ($R = 1.6\text{k}\Omega, C = 10\text{nF}$).
  • The Result: Cleanly extracted and amplified the $1250\text{Hz}\text{–}3666\text{Hz}$ signal window with $120\text{dB}$ mid-band gain while sharply attenuating DC, $100\text{Hz}$, and $20\text{kHz}$ interference without saturating the op-amp outputs.
  • What This Artifact Demonstrates: Multi-pole active/passive filter synthesis, Bode corner-frequency design, high-gain amplifier staging, and signal-to-noise optimization.

Artifact 3: Single-Supply Light-Following Robot Filter & Virtual Ground Biasing

  • Standalone Write-Up: Open Artifact 3 Full Page →
  • The Problem: Process a $1\text{kHz}$ pulsed optical signal (I1 = 0.1 mA) for a light-following robot operating from a single $9\text{V}$ battery (V1 = 9V) and $0\text{V}$ ground, while rejecting steady-state ambient room lighting that would otherwise saturate or clip the signal against the $0\text{V}$ rail.
  • My Contribution: I designed an AC-coupled inverting op-amp stage ($R_4 = 10\text{M}\Omega, R_5 = 50\text{M}\Omega$, voltage gain $|A_v| = 5\text{ V/V}$) where the op-amp rails sit at $9\text{V}$ and $0\text{V}$ while a matched $100\text{k}\Omega$ divider ($R_7, R_8$) biases the non-inverting input (+) to a $+4.5\text{V}$ virtual ground. I paired this with input ($C_1 = 1\ \mu\text{F}$) and output ($C_2 = 1\ \mu\text{F}, R_9 = 1\text{M}\Omega$) AC-coupling networks.
  • The Result: Enabled full symmetric AC signal swing centered at $+4.5\text{V}$ inside the op-amp without rail clipping, and delivered a clean, $0\text{V}$-referenced output signal (out) completely free of ambient DC room-light interference.
  • What This Artifact Demonstrates: Single-supply op-amp biasing, DC blocking / AC restoration, high-impedance optical sensor conditioning, and practical robotics hardware design.

Artifact 4: NGspice Netlist Verification, Capacitor Grounding Audit & Multi-Pole Revision

  • Standalone Write-Up: Open Artifact 4 Full Page →
  • The Problem: Early iterations of the optical receiver netlist and schematic risked shunting AC signals or locking op-amp rails due to mis-grounded coupling capacitors (C6/C7 and C23/C24) and strict requirements to preserve starter components (V1, I1, and R1) without modification.
  • My Contribution: I performed a comprehensive node-by-node audit between the schematic and NGspice netlist—confirming that all series coupling capacitors were routed inline without grounding them, verifying that shunt bypass/low-pass capacitors terminated properly at ground (0), and upgrading single-pole sections into 3-stage RC cascades based on simulation diagnostics.
  • The Result: Eliminated schematic-to-netlist topology discrepancies, achieved steep 4th-order roll-off on both sides of the passband, and produced a verified netlist that passed all Milestone 1 simulation benchmarks.
  • What This Artifact Demonstrates: Systematic hardware/simulation troubleshooting, SPICE netlist fluency, strict interface compliance, and feedback-driven iterative engineering.

4. Evidence of Revision Based on Feedback

This portfolio and the underlying circuit designs incorporate direct revisions from instructor, TA, and peer feedback:

  1. Portfolio Structure, Target Role & Navigation Revision:
    • Before: My initial Hugo site used a minimal blog list with only two visible posts, lacked an explicit target role banner and table of contents, and used inconsistent section headings (such as “Context” and “Procedure”).
    • After (Revised): I adapted the portfolio into a structured engineering resume & showcase featuring an explicit Target Role (Security Infrastructure & Data Center Hardware Engineer), a sticky navigation bar and Organized Table of Contents, and four complete EC EN 340 artifacts standardized around The Problem, My Contribution, The Result, and What This Artifact Demonstrates.
  2. Restoring & Expanding Overwritten Netlist Artifact (commit 7b2ba54 → Artifact 1 & Artifact 4):
    • Before: My earlier SPICE netlist write-up (“EC EN 340 Artifact 2: SPICE Circuit Simulation”, explaining the $v_p = +1.65\text{V} / v_n = -1.65\text{V}$ ground placement between R2 and R3 and proper routing of C6 and C7) had been overwritten when second-artifact.md was replaced with the Light-Following Robot Filter.
    • After (Revised): I recovered that technical analysis from version control and expanded it into Artifact 1 (Rail Splitter & Ripple Decoupling) and Artifact 4 (Netlist Verification & Capacitor Routing Audit), complete with cropped and full-system schematics.
  3. Technical Circuit Revisions in NGspice:
    • Added the 3-stage $10\ \Omega / 159\ \mu\text{F}$ RC ripple filter ahead of the R2/R3 rail splitter to suppress the $1481\text{Hz}$ supply ripple.
    • Expanded the input high-pass and output low-pass filters into 3-stage passive RC cascades ($15\text{nF}/10.6\text{k}\Omega$ and $1.6\text{k}\Omega/10\text{nF}$) to sharpen out-of-band noise rejection at $100\text{Hz}$ and $20\text{kHz}$.
    • Added the output AC-coupling restoration network ($C_2 = 1\ \mu\text{F}, R_9 = 1\text{M}\Omega$) on the $9\text{V}$ single-supply robot filter so the output swings around $0\text{V}$ instead of riding on $+4.5\text{V}$ DC.

5. Design Journey Note: Start of Semester vs. Now

What I can now do that I could not do at the beginning of the semester:

At the beginning of the semester in EC EN 340, I could solve basic textbook resistor networks and ideal op-amp equations on paper, but I could not design a multi-stage analog front-end that survived real-world physical imperfections like single-supply rail limits, power-line ripple, and overwhelming ambient optical interference.

Specifically, I can now:

  1. Design Multi-Stage Active & Passive Bandpass Filters to Exact Specifications: I can calculate RC pole and zero frequencies ($f_c = \frac{1}{2\pi RC}$), cascade multiple passive and active stages, and distribute $120\text{dB}$ of gain across dual op-amps to recover a $1\text{pA}$ signal inside a strict $1250\text{Hz}\text{–}3666\text{Hz}$ window while rejecting interferences $10^6\times$ larger.
  2. Engineer Single-Supply Virtual Grounds & Power Integrity Networks: Rather than relying on ideal $\pm V_{CC}$ bench supplies, I can bias single-supply op-amps ($9\text{V}$ or $3.3\text{V}$) to a stable mid-rail virtual ground ($+4.5\text{V}$ or $\pm 1.65\text{V}$), decouple noisy power rails with multi-stage RC filters and dual-decade bypass capacitors, and AC-couple inputs and outputs to prevent rail clipping.
  3. Debug & Verify Complex Topologies in NGspice Before Building Hardware: I can translate schematic constraints into SPICE netlists, diagnose subtle node-grounding bugs, and use simulation data to iteratively refine a circuit before committing to a physical breadboard or PCB.

6. Connection to BYU Aims

My engineering work in EC EN 340 and my broader preparation as a Computer Engineering & Cybersecurity student directly connect to the Aims of a BYU Education (https://aims.byu.edu/):

  • Intellectually Enlarging: BYU emphasizes uniting rigorous academic theory with practical competence. In EC EN 340, bridging mathematical transfer functions and Bode plots with real-world non-idealities—such as filtering out a $1481\text{Hz}$ power-supply ripple or preventing single-supply op-amp saturation—taught me how to think across levels of abstraction. As a future Security Infrastructure Engineer, this ability to connect physical-layer hardware realities (power integrity, signal noise, hardware diagnostics) with higher-level network virtualization and security architecture is essential.
  • Lifelong Learning and Service & Character Building: Engineering is ultimately a stewardship of trust. Whether I am mentoring and supervising student IT technicians on campus, methodically auditing an NGspice netlist so a circuit operates safely and reliably, or securing enterprise server infrastructure using principles from my CompTIA Security+ and Network+ training, I strive to practice disciplined verification, continuous learning, and dependable service to others.
